job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in Madrid with my parents and my grandmother, in a flat in Carabanchel. I'm up at seven, and the first thing I do is open an AI assistant to help me plan my day and draft messages. By ten I'm working on a small drone project on the balcony, and in the afternoon I send applications. On Sundays we have a big lunch after Mass. I finished electrical and computer engineering seven months ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about your final project and your internships.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My final project was the firmware for a drone that sprays crops, so farmers use less chemical, and it got a top mark. I did one internship at an aerospace supplier, testing circuit boards, and one at a software firm, writing small tools. I love when the code makes something move in the real world. I've sent about fifty applications and had four interviews, but no offer yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, we get on with it. I use AI every day already, and it makes me faster but not smarter. I'd tell friends to use it, but not to treat it as a miracle, and that people still have to do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm about the AI side and impatient about the job side. Four interviews, no offer. The market has plenty of openings, so I think it's a matter of time and fit. A plateau means my skills stay valuable, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, aim at aerospace and drone firms, and keep improving the spraying drone. I'd also post a video of it flying over a test field, because a video says more than a CV. I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a small farm in Toledo, and ask to test the drone on his land. That could become a real product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit restless. I feel lucky, because my family's support and savings give me time. I'd just like to begin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your daily work already uses AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you start your own business if the job didn't come?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your time in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. I like the idea of making something and selling it. The free market rewards people who build things, and I'd prefer to work for myself than wait for a favour. But I'd start with a job to learn how real companies run, and then decide.

say: I'd say it's fine and we get on with it: AI makes me **faster** but not smarter.
I'd tell friends people still have to do the **work**.
think: I'm calm about AI and **impatient** about the job side.
A plateau keeps my skills **valuable**, and I like that.
do: Post a **video** of my spraying drone flying over a test field.
Test the drone on my uncle's **farm** in Toledo.
feel: **Calm** and a bit restless, and lucky to have family support.
S0.quote: A video says more than a CV.
fieldNote: She uses **AI** daily and treats it as a helper.
Her instinct is to build and **sell**, matching her free-market leanings.
Calm rests on savings and plenty of openings, while the delay makes her impatient.

steps.text: Apply to aerospace and drone firms around Madrid every week
Test the spraying drone on my uncle's farm in Toledo
Use an AI assistant to speed up my firmware testing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when technology moves, and people who learn fast do well. I'd say firms should invest in training, and the state shouldn't block them. I'd also say that families and communities have to help those who find it hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a squeeze, but I'm well placed. Writing test code and basic firmware are junior tasks, and the tools do them fast. But I use the tools already and I can work with hardware, which software alone can't touch. That's my advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd target roles where software meets hardware, like embedded systems, drones and robotics. I'd get certified in a drone licence, and I'd show a clean demo of my sprayer. I'd also start offering small firmware fixes to local companies, because there's money in that. And I'd keep using the AI tools to build faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly uneasy, but excited. It's like a race that I think I can win, if I don't stumble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Test code, first drafts, simple drivers. Software does these quickly. What software can't do easily is debug a motor that sparks on the bench, and I've done that, and I'd say it's hard to fake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the strongest version of your plan be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd combine hardware skill, tool skill and a product that real people use. If one fails, the others hold. Diversified skills are like diversified savings: they protect you.

say: I'd say technology moves and people who **learn fast** do well.
I'd say firms should invest in **training** and families should help those who struggle.
think: I'd feel a **squeeze**, but I'm well placed with hardware skills.
Software alone can't touch **hardware**, and that's my advantage.
do: Target **embedded systems**, drones and robotics roles.
Get a **drone licence** and show a clean demo.
Offer small **firmware fixes** to local companies.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, but excited, like a race I think I can win.
S1.quote: Diversified skills are like diversified savings: they protect you.
fieldNote: Her **hardware** edge is her main argument.
She thinks like an owner: several skills, several sources of **income**.
Her public line mixes free markets with family duty.

steps.text: Take the drone pilot licence exam this spring
Apply to embedded and robotics firms near Madrid
Sell small firmware fixes to local companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious, and everyone should be honest about it. Families and communities must stay together, and governments should keep markets working but protect the weakest. I'd say it plainly at church and at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. The thinking side of my field is done within two years, and I'd have no seniority. Even robots come three years after, so my drone work isn't safe for long. I'd feel like I have a short time to find something sturdy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small company at once, a drone service for farms, using my uncle's land and the contacts he has. I'd also keep applying for jobs, as a safety net. I'd put my savings into a drone and basic equipment, which I think is a smart risk. And I'd lean on my family for rent, which isn't pride, just sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but alive. It's like standing on a diving board: scary, but I'm ready to jump. I'd feel better once I had a plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years, then robots. What is your first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might delay them. I want a family by thirty, but I'd want to be steady in my work first. I'd talk to my future husband, if I had one by then, about taking risks together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this change your plans to marry and have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My first month is for a plan. Week one: write down what I can do, what it costs and who needs it. Week two: talk to farmers. Week three: buy the first drone. Week four: fly it for a paying customer.

say: I'd say this is serious and we should be **honest** about it.
I'd say governments should keep markets working but protect the **weakest**.
think: The thinking side of my field is done in two years and I'd have **no seniority**.
I'd have a short time to find something **sturdy**.
do: Start a small **drone service** for farms using my uncle's land.
Keep applying for jobs as a **safety net**.
Put savings into a drone and basic **equipment**.
feel: **Anxious** but alive, like standing on a diving board.
S2.quote: My first month is for a plan. Week one: write down what I can do, what it costs and who needs it.
fieldNote: Her answer to anxiety is a **concrete plan**, week by week.
She is willing to take a smart **risk** with savings.
Family plans may be delayed, which she says openly.

steps.text: Register a small drone spraying service and sign two farms
Keep applying to embedded firms as a safety net
Buy a first spraying drone with 4000 euros of savings
Ask my parents to cover rent for six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's long enough to build something real. Firms should hire and train, and young people should start companies. I'd say politely that the state should not get in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy, but excited. I could work for a few years, learn how real companies run, save, then launch my own product by thirty. That seems like a good path in a fast world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job at a robotics or drone firm, learn the business, then start my own company on the side. I'd build the spraying drone into a product, with my uncle as the first customer. I'd save money, and get engaged around twenty-six. I'd also use AI to write most of my code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. It feels like a start-up with a deadline. I like deadlines, and I like having time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work first, to learn, and build on the side. If the side project reaches real customers, I'd switch. In a world where jobs can disappear, owning something is safer than being a good employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide between a job and your own company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can also help my parents and grandmother. I'd buy them a better flat or at least help with repairs. That's what family is for, and having time to do it matters to me.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to build something **real**.
I'd say the state should not get in the way of **young companies**.
think: I'd be uneasy but **excited**: I could launch my own product by thirty.
That seems like a good path in a **fast world**.
do: Take a job at a **robotics or drone** firm and learn the business.
Turn the spraying drone into a **product** with my uncle as the first customer.
Save money and get **engaged** around twenty-six.
feel: Mostly **good**, like a start-up with a deadline.
S3.quote: In a world where jobs can disappear, owning something is safer than being a good employee.
fieldNote: Time lets her take a **job plus side company**, one feeding the other.
She also plans to help her parents and grandmother.

steps.text: Accept a job at a robotics or drone firm in Madrid
Build the spraying drone into a product for farms
Save a third of every pay cheque for the company
Plan an engagement and help my parents repair the flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should build as much as we can. I'd say family, work and faith give a person a base, and from a base you can take risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. By 33 I could be married, with children, and have a small company that employs several people. The tools will change many times, but I enjoy learning. I'd feel secure, as long as I keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for two or three years, then launch the drone company, hire a few engineers, and use AI heavily. I'd buy a house in a quieter neighbourhood in Madrid, and maybe a plot near Toledo. I'd keep going to Mass, spend Sundays with family, and save a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Happy, even. It feels like the plan I'd have made anyway, but with more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What does your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait for permission. Learn something, build something, and ask older people for advice. And remember you're not alone, because family and neighbours are the first safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who is more afraid than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell them that fear is normal. I'm adaptive, but I'm not fearless. I just prefer to move than to freeze.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and we should build as much as we can.
I'd say family, work and faith give a **base** for taking risks.
think: I'm **calm**: by 33 I could be married with a small company that employs several people.
I enjoy **learning**, so I'd feel secure.
do: Work two or three years, then **launch** the drone company.
Buy a house in a quieter **neighbourhood** and maybe a plot near Toledo.
Keep going to **Mass**, spend Sundays with family and save.
feel: **Hopeful**, even happy, like the plan I'd have made anyway.
S4.quote: I'm adaptive, but I'm not fearless. I just prefer to move than to freeze.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her merge **faith**, family and business into one plan.
She admits fear and says her only difference is **movement**.
She describes the family as the first safety net.

steps.text: Work two years, then launch the drone company
Buy a house in Madrid and a small plot near Toledo
Marry and have children around 28 to 30
Keep Sunday Mass and family lunches as a fixed routine

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have only a short time to find something sturdy, and my family would feel it too. What would help is room to start small companies, honest talk from firms, and a first job that lets me learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Being adaptive doesn't mean being safe. I just prefer making a plan to staring at the news. I use AI every day, and I'm still afraid of the fast one.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive doesn't mean being safe. I just prefer making a plan to staring at the news.
portrait: Elena is **23**, an electrical and computer engineering graduate in Madrid, living with her parents and grandmother.
She uses AI **every day**, builds a crop-spraying drone and thinks like an owner.
She leans towards free markets and tradition: family, faith, work and **ownership** shape her plans.
Her mood follows the clock: calm in slow worlds and **anxious** when AGI is two years away.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because she'd have only a short time to find something sturdy.
whatWouldHelp: Room to start **small companies**, honest talk from firms and a first job that lets her learn.
